title: Significance of Myo7a isoforms in hair cell function
text:
Hearing relies on specialized sensory cells in the inner ear known as hair cells,
which require the protein Myosin 7a (MYO7A) for normal function and sound
detection. Mutations in the MYO7A gene are a leading cause of inherited hearing
loss. This project investigates the distinct isoforms of MYO7A, their specific roles
in hair cell function and hearing sensitivity, and the molecular mechanisms that
regulate their expression. Understanding which isoforms are essential and how
they are controlled will inform the development of targeted gene therapies aimed
at restoring hearing in individuals with MYO7A-related deafness.

title: Aged T-cell-derived cytokines impact meningeal lymphatics and contribute to AD
text:
Many age-related neurodegenerative diseases—including Alzheimer's disease (AD)—are associated with
misfolded protein deposition that promote inflammatory responses, neuronal dysfunction, and cognitive deficits.
In this proposal we will address the hypothesis that aging immune cells (in particular, aging T lymphocytes)
produce inflammatory molecule, IFN, which interacts with brain-draining lymphatic vessels in the borders of the
brain and disrupts their function, subsequently leading to dysfunctional clearance of the brain's waste. We will
assess the mechanism and therapeutic approaches to target this route as means to ameliorate Alzheimer's
disease progression.

title: Translational and genomic pediatric cancer epidemiology training program
text:
Childhood cancer is the leading cause of death due to disease in children the United States while childhood
cancer survivors, which number over 350,000, face lifelong increased morbidity and mortality. This training
program equips researchers and physician-scientists with experience in classical epidemiology, genomic
epidemiology, clinical investigations, and complementary laboratory studies relevant to childhood cancer
etiology, outcome of therapy, and survivorship.

title: Examining Peer Influences in Alcohol and Sexual Violence among Marines Using a Dyadic Multimethod Approach
text:
Alcohol misuse and sexual assault are problematic among men in the US Marine Corps and efficacious
prevention approaches remain elusive. The proposed multi-method project will address critical gaps in
knowledge by obtaining an event-level understanding of the role of alcohol in sexual violence perpetration among
dyads of Marine men who drink together by using in vivo and in vitro assessment methods.

title: Genomics
text: ABSTRACT – GENOMICS SHARED RESOURCE The Genomics Shared Resource is managed by the Cancer Center and provides full nucleic acid-to-data services, from library preparation to basic data analysis, focused primarily on next-generation sequencing (NGS) applications. Most of the services currently offered by the Core have been added in the last 5 years following the recruitment of Dr. Brian James as the Facility Director in 2013. The Core upgrades in the past funding period include Illumina-based sequencing on the NextSeq 500, automated library preparation using the Eppendorf epMotion 5075, single-cell sequencing on the 10x Genomics Chromium and Bio-Rad ddSeq platforms, and human cell line authentication using the Promega GenePrint 10 system. In addition to RNA-seq, services offered include ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, exome-seq, CRISPR libraries, and phage display libraries. Since the Genomics Core began offering NGS service, it has worked with the majority of Cancer Center member labs. In many cases, this was the lab's first experience with high-throughput sequencing technology, and the Core was instrumental in helping the investigators to design, execute, and interpret these experiments. Integrated basic NGS bioinformatic analysis is included as part of the service. This is a critical component in assuring the quality of the data produced and facilitating the eventual scientific success of the Center members. The Genomics Core provides broad support, with 41 Center labs having used the Core in the last 5 years, and it has supported at least 46 cancer-related publications.

title: The role of the ventral CA1 in distinct social representations
text:
Inability to interpret and remember emotional social interactions are prevalent symptoms in many
neuropsychiatric disorders including autism-spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia, which lack effective
treatment. The goal of this proposal is to identify the circuit and molecular substrates underlying the formation of
valence-associated social memories and uncover the cell types which support changing valence association
over time. Mechanistic insight into the neural basis of social valence association will set the foundation for the
development of therapeutic treatments for its deficits.

title: Coordinating and Data Management Center  for Translational and Basic Science Research in Early Lesions
text:
We propose to establish a Coordinating and Data Management Center (CDMC) for the Program on the
Translational and Basic Science Research in Early Lesions (TBEL), which is being established to
undertake various translational and basic science studies to provide fundamental knowledge on the
mechanisms driving or restraining early cancers. The proposed CDMC will support critical administrative,
regulatory, managerial, logistics, data-analytic, computational, and financial functions of the TBEL
Program.

title: Genetic pleiotropy across pediatric cancers, and cancer-related outcomes
text:
RELEVANCE
Despite advances in pediatric oncology treatment and research, our understanding of the genetic etiology of
pediatric cancers remains incomplete. We propose to undertake a first-of-its-kind analysis of pediatric cancer
pleiotropy, identifying genetic variations that contribute to risks for multiple pediatric cancer types. We will also
examine the shared heritability of pediatric cancers with the first comprehensive study of global pleiotropy
patterns for pediatric cancer risk, and develop enhanced genetic risk score tools with pleiotropic risk variants to
better predict who may develop pediatric cancer and inform personalized treatment, surveillance, and
interventions to reduce morbidity and mortality after pediatric cancer diagnosis.

title: Center for Multiparametric Imaging of Tumor Immune Microenvironments
text:
The Center for Multiparametric Imaging of Tumor Immune Microenvironments (C-MITIE) will define
physical and molecular barriers to effective anti-tumor immune responses and therapies. As an
integrated team we will advance and develop state-of-the-art live cell and tissue optical imaging
platforms and quantitative analyses to define the principal physical barriers that limit effective anti-tumor
immunity and immunotherapy. This will facilitate design criteria for novel immunotherapy regimens and
next-generation cell-based immunotherapies for cancer patients.

title: Regulation of the functional expression of the TRPM7 chanzyme essential for Mg2+ homeostasis in mouse oocytes and cleaving embryos to improve assisted reproductive technologies and modulate fertility
text:
The proposed project is relevant to public health because it focuses on the factors that
modulate the functional expression of the TRPM7 chanzyme, an essential regulator of
Mg2+ homeostasis in embryos and preimplantation development. Once we identify these
regulatory factors and their signaling pathways, there is potential for advancing in vitro
culture systems for gametes and embryos, our understanding of embryo metabolism, and
improving nutritional recommendations to maximize fertility. Thus, the proposed research
is relevant to the part of the NIH’s mission that pertains to developing fundamental
knowledge that will enhance health and reduce disease burden.

title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic FactorsDriving Clonal Evolution and Disease Progression in Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
text:
The overall objective of this proposal is to determine how inflammatory cytokine signaling pathways intersect
with cell intrinsic/extrinsic mechanisms to drive clonal expansion and MPN disease progression. Our proposed
projects leverage established collaborations and incorporate state-of-the-art approaches to foster synergy beyond what could be achieved independently. These studies will provide insights with the potential to lead directly
to improved therapies for MPN patients.

title: The Role of Air Quality and Built Environment in Social Isolation and Cognitive Function among Rural, Racially/Ethnically Diverse Residents at Risk for Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Rural communities experiencing repeated intermittent exposures to air pollution during
agricultural burns often face social isolation, and both are linked to increased risk for
Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). However, the intersection of these factors,
combined with the influence of rural built and social environments on cognitive function have not
been studied, particularly in the context of racially/ethnically diverse farmworkers who already
face increased ADRD risk. This proposed research will inform the design of public health
interventions that can diminish the threat of ADRD in rural settings and save healthcare dollars.

title: Project 1: Nuclear Imaging and Phage Pharmacokinetics
text: SUMMARY There is a resurgence of interest in bacteriophages (phages) as treatments for MDR/XDR-PA pneumonia in people with cystic fibrosis (CF) and other settings. Most recent cases, including clinical trials and individual compassionate use cases, involve multiple phages given together (“phage cocktails”). However, the clinical development of phage therapy is stymied by a limited understanding of the link between phage dose and infection site concentrations (i.e., pharmacokinetics [PK]). Cu Developing a PK mathematical model requires many in vivo phage concentration samples, but it is logistically infeasible to accomplish this with plaque assays and qPCR. Consequently, PK studies are rarely performed for single phages, let alone cocktails. To establish the mathematical PK link between phage dose and target site concentrations, the field urgently needs faster, high-throughput ways to measure phage concentrations to inform translational PK mathematical models. Positron Emission Tomography (PET) can provide highly quantitative, real-time, continuous monitoring of drug distribution, accumulation, and clearance. PET imaging of 64Cu-labeled adeno associated viral (AAV) developed by the Ferrara lab has been successful in quantifying AAV. To-date, PET has not been optimized for phage therapy. Our existing 125I-radiolabeling strategies successfully quantified phage organ concentration to inform the first physiologically based PK (PBPK) model of phage, but had several limitations. These strategies can be meaningfully innovated to improve sample frequency and resolution through PET imaging of 64Cu-phage. Further, by co-labeling 64Cu-phage DNA with a near infrared (NIR) fluorescent dye, SYTO63, we can elucidate distribution of phage at the tissue level using traditional microscopy and histology techniques. For these studies, we will use both wild type (WT) and CFTR-/- (CFTR-KO) rats, a rodent model of CF, as well as the KIMC1 cocktail phages, a cocktail specifically developed to target PA isolates collected from pwCF. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that PET imaging can be used to quantify phage distribution and to establish the PK of phages and phage cocktails. To test this, In Aim 1 we will establish broadly applicable single and multimodal PET and fluorescence labeling methods for phages. Then in Aim 2 we will establish a dynamic PET imaging method for high-resolution quantification of phage biodistribution and tissue target site localization. Finally, in Aim 3 we will characterize distribution, accumulation, and degradation kinetics of multiple phages administered as a cocktail. The successful development of nuclear imaging protocols for fast, easily translatable methods of phage PK will empower the development of phage therapy for CF lung infections and other indications.

title: Evaluation of digital angiogenesis in scleroderma by molecular imaging
text:
This project introduces a new way to look at small blood vessels in the hands of scleroderma patients using
advanced imaging technology. By combining specialized cameras and detailed 3D scanners, we can see how
new blood vessels form and compare these images with MRI scans that show blood vessel damage, scarring,
and oxygen levels. This study aims to create new tools to help doctors prevent and treat severe finger sores in
scleroderma patients, ultimately improving their quality of life.

title: Core D-Get IN
text:
GET iN Narrative
The GET iN Core generates viral and nonviral constructs for delivering genes and proteins into cells and skin.
The Core provides counseling to scientists and hosts an educational program about gene manipulation, gene
editing, and delivering genetic materials into skin.

title: Polymeric Micelles for Targeted Delivery of Contrast Agents Through the Nose-to-Brain Route in Image-Guided Brain Cancer Surgery
text:
The removal of a tumor is an important stage of treatment, as it allows the extraction of a large volume of
tumor tissue, the reduction of intracranial pressure, the decrease of neurological deficit and the establishment
of an exact tumor phenotype to solve the question of further treatment tactics. Modern research has shown
that the size of tumor resection is reliably correlated with the life expectancy of patients. In the case of diffuse
astrocytomas with a low degree of malignancy, total tumor removal is a key prognostic factor as it effectively
reduces the risk of malignant tumor transformation. For adult patients with brainstem high-grade gliomas, one
of the rarest and deadliest forms of brain cancer, surgically removing the entire tumor may add many months
or potentially years of survival beyond that offered by radiation and chemotherapy. The main paradigm of brain
tumor surgery is the maximal removal of the tumor with minimal risk of damage to functionally significant areas
of the brain. However, the extraction of a tumor in the white light of a microscope can only achieve a maximum
resection in 23–50% of cases. This contributes to maintaining a high interest in the development of
intraoperative technologies that allow the differentiation of tumors from surrounding tissues.
In this proposed study, we aspire to develop, characterize, and evaluate intranasally delivered tumor-targeting
polymeric micelles carrying a self-quenched near-infrared (NIR) imaging agent on its potential in brain imaging
and neurosurgical guidance during brain tumor surgery. This system is designed to switch “off” fluorescence
signals until the micelles arrive at tumor tissues and begin to release an imaging agent as a monomeric form,
resulting in strong fluorescence (“on”) signals on tumor tissues.
We believe that the polymeric micelles proposed in this study will offer high sensitivity and specificity in
imaging brain tumor for distinguishing tumor tissues from surrounding white matter and ultimately improve
surgical outcomes and patient survival, potentially adding decades of quality life.

title: Discerning the role of CDK10 in driving aggressiveness and disparities of triple negative breast cancer
text:
Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly aggressive disease with limited treatment options that
disproportionately affects young and African American women. We found that CDK10 controls the growth of
TNBC cells and that it may be more active in tumors from Black compared to White patients. This project will
determine if CDK10 is a major driver of TNBC aggressiveness and the racial disparities in this disease with the
expectation that CDK10 could be a novel drug target for treating TNBC.

title: Neural Circuits for Stress-Impaired Extinction Learning
text:
Therapeutic interventions, such as exposure therapy, reduce pathological fear in patients with anxiety
disorders—but this fear reduction is often transient and vulnerable to relapse. Stress undermines exposure
therapy by disabling brain circuits critical for extinction learning. The long-term goal of this project is to
understand the circuit and cellular mechanisms by which stress undermines extinction learning, a program of
study that is essential for improving the long-term efficacy of exposure-based therapies .

title: Rational optimization of combinatorial therapies for the treatment of rare cystic fibrosis variants
text:
Project Narrative.
Several recently approved therapeutics have revolutionized the treatment of cystic fibrosis, which is a common
genetic disease caused by a spectrum of mutations within the CFTR gene. However, the optimal combination of
drugs for each patient depends on the nature of their specific genetic variations, and the optimal therapeutic
combinations have yet to be determined for the hundreds of known CF mutations. The proposed investigations
will utilize a combination of emerging techniques to comprehensively match current medications to these
mutations and help to target new drugs as they come to market.

title: Deciphering Male- and Female-coordinated Gating Mechanisms that Ensure Plant Reproductive Success
text:
Public Health Relevance/Narrative
Reproduction in flowering plants produces seeds thus provides for global nutritional needs, food
security, and ensures ecological balance that is important for climate health. Yet the process
involves complex male-female interplays and is highly sensitive to the environment, such as high
and low temperatures, drought and flood, and reproductive failure devastates seed yields.
Understanding the molecular mechanisms that lead to plant reproductive success will help
designs of counter measures to reproductive loss and therefore relevant to NIH commitment to
fundamental research in model organisms whose success ultimately protects human health.
